extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in publication ethics and mathematics retractions
extracted.subtask_description: A blog-style compilation and commentary on multiple retractions in the journal Applied Mathematics Letters, highlighting causes (nonsense mathematics, falsification, unsubstantiated claims), publisher responses, and implications for peer review and publishing ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical coherence / proofs must make sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of it makes 'no sense mathematically'. 'Not a single statement in the author’s “proof” makes sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitted proofs and constructions must be logically coherent and intelligible to competent mathematicians; nonsensical or internally inconsistent arguments are an immediate red flag and indicate failure of quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: No falsified mathematical findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction notice states the 'authors have falsified mathematical findings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication or deliberate falsification of results is a serious ethical breach and grounds for retraction; editors and reviewers must guard against data/finding fabrication in mathematical and applied work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be substantiated
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper 'made unsubstantiated claims regarding Euclid’s parallel postulate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide rigorous justification and evidence for claims, especially when they concern foundational results; unsupported assertions are unacceptable and justify correction or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust peer review and editorial oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction notice and commentary note that the problematic material 'was not detected during the submission process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals must ensure competent, thorough peer review and editorial scrutiny so that nonsensical, falsified, or unsubstantiated work is caught before publication; cursory or ineffective review is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction, correction, and apology as part of remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied Mathematics Letters retracted papers and 'apologies are offered to readers of the journal that this was not detected during the submission process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When serious problems are discovered post-publication, the appropriate remedies include formal retraction/correction notices, clear explanations to readers, and apologies when editorial failure occurred; publishers should correct the record promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against publishing pseudoscience or ideologically-driven work
rubrics_metrics.description: Posts reference 'Intelligent Design-friendly' papers and articles claiming spiritual origins or violations of the second law of thermodynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reviewers should be vigilant about submissions motivated by ideology or pseudoscience; extraordinary or contrarian claims that conflict with well-established science require especially rigorous scrutiny and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: The site tags include 'not reproducible' and the posts emphasize inability to make sense of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results and constructions should be verifiable by other researchers; work that cannot be reproduced or whose steps cannot be checked undermines trust and may justify retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher transparency and accountability (including legal/financial remediation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elsevier 'will issue an apology and pay $10,000 in legal fees' in one discussed case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers bear responsibility for mistakes in editorial processes; transparent acknowledgement, public apology, and—where appropriate—financial/legal remediation are part of accountable handling of serious publication errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of outlets that facilitate publication of dodgy work
rubrics_metrics.description: The post 'How to get dodgy math papers published: An algorithm' and references to venues like Rejecta Mathematica question where flawed work may be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid submitting to venues with weak or absent peer review; readers and indexers should be cautious about outlets known to publish low-quality or non-reviewed material, and journals should avoid becoming such outlets.
